title: House Robber
directAnswer: For each house you either skip it (keep dp[i-1]) or rob it (take nums[i] + dp[i-2]) — you can't rob two adjacent houses. The recurrence is dp[i] = max(dp[i-1], nums[i] + dp[i-2]). Memoize the recursion, then collapse it to two rolling variables for O(n) time and O(1) space.

rules: At each house make a binary choice: **skip** it (carry `dp[i-1]`) or **rob** it (`nums[i] + dp[i-2]`). Take the max.
Robbing house `i` forbids house `i-1`, so the money before it must come from `dp[i-2]`, not `dp[i-1]`.
This is `max`, not sum — you're **maximizing loot**, the opposite of Climbing Stairs' counting.
Two rolling variables suffice: `rob1` = best up to i-2, `rob2` = best up to i-1. Slide them each step.
Handle empty input (return 0) and a single house (return nums[0]) — the loop handles the rest cleanly if seeded with zeros.
whenToUse: Maximize a sum over a line of items where picking one forbids its neighbor
Each decision is a local take/skip with a constraint on adjacency
The optimum at i is built from the optimum a fixed number of items back
No grouping or ordering freedom — items are processed left to right
antiSignals: Houses are in a circle (first and last are adjacent) → House Robber II, run it twice
Houses form a tree, not a line → House Robber III, post-order DP
You're counting arrangements, not maximizing a value → that's a sum DP like Climbing Stairs
Picking an item forbids a *range*, not just one neighbor → weighted interval scheduling
remember.takeaway: House Robber is the archetypal 'take-or-skip with a gap' DP. The instant you see 'can't pick adjacent', reach for dp[i] = max(skip, take + dp[i-2]). It generalizes directly to the circular and tree variants, and the rolling-variable compression is the same O(1)-space trick as Climbing Stairs.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you can model a constrained optimization as a per-element take/skip decision, write the max recurrence with the correct i-2 dependency, and compress to O(1) space.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Assuming the answer is just 'rob every other house' (a greedy that fails on [2,1,1,2]), or pulling the 'take' branch from dp[i-1] instead of dp[i-2].
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: Disprove the greedy with a counterexample out loud, derive the recurrence cleanly, then optimize to two variables and note the circular/tree follow-ups build on this exact core.

problemStatement:
You are a professional robber planning to rob houses along a street. Each house has a certain amount of money stashed, given by the array `nums`.

The only constraint stopping you is that **adjacent houses have connected security systems** — robbing two directly adjacent houses on the same night will automatically alert the police.

Return the ***maximum amount of money*** you can rob tonight without alerting the police.
understanding: Choose a subset of houses with no two adjacent, maximizing the total money. It's a max-weight independent set on a path graph — but because it's a simple line, a left-to-right DP solves it in linear time.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can I rob non-adjacent houses freely?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes — the only rule is no two directly adjacent houses. Houses i and i+2 are both fair game.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can the money in a house be zero or negative?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Values are 0..400, so non-negative. Robbing never hurts the total, but a 0-value house still can't sit next to another robbed house.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Is the street a line or a circle?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: A line here — the first and last houses are NOT adjacent. The circular version is House Robber II.

clarifyingQuestions.question: What should I return for an empty street?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: 0. With a single house, return its value. Seeding the rolling variables with zeros handles both without special cases.

examples.explanation: Rob house 0 (1) and house 2 (3) → 4. Robbing 1 and 3 gives only 3.
Rob houses 0 and 3 → 2 + 2 = 4. The naive 'every other house' (2 + 1 = 3) is worse — proof that greedy fails.

diagrams.title: Picking the right approach
diagrams.caption: The decision tree to run before writing code. House Robber lands on the rolling-variables branch.

approaches.name: Brute Force — Recursion Over Take/Skip
approaches.whenToMention: Say this first to expose the decision tree and justify the recurrence, then flag the exponential blowup before moving on.
hints: Stand at house i and ask: what are my only two choices, and what do they each forbid?
If you rob i you collect nums[i] but must jump to i+2; if you skip i you move to i+1 with nothing collected. Take the better of the two.
Write rob(i) = max(nums[i] + rob(i+2), rob(i+1)), returning 0 once i runs past the end.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Each call branches into two (rob-and-skip-two vs skip-one), forming a tree with up to ~2ⁿ nodes. Recursion depth is O(n) for the stack.
approaches.explanation:
Frame the street as a sequence of binary decisions. Standing at house `i`, you either **rob it** — collect `nums[i]` and you're forced to skip to `i+2` — or **skip it** and move to `i+1` with nothing. The best you can do from `i` is the max of those two futures.

**The mental shift: from 'which subset?' to 'what's my next move?'.** The brute-force instinct is to enumerate all valid subsets, but that's hard to reason about. Reframing it as a per-house take/skip turns the whole problem into one clean recurrence with two branches. Each branch encodes the adjacency rule automatically: robbing jumps by two, skipping jumps by one, so you can never select neighbors.

**Why greedy ('rob every other house') is wrong.** It's the trap answer. On `[2, 1, 1, 2]` alternating gives `2 + 1 = 3`, but robbing the two ends gives `2 + 2 = 4`. The optimal choice at each house depends on the whole rest of the street, which is exactly why we need DP and not a fixed pattern.

**Why we don't ship this.** `rob(i+2)` and `rob(i+1)` overlap heavily — the same suffix gets recomputed across branches, so the tree is exponential. State the cost, then cache it.
approaches.insight: Notice that `rob(i)` depends only on `i`, yet the naive tree solves the same `rob(i)` many times from different paths. That overlap is the universal cue that a recursion is secretly a polynomial DP waiting for a cache.

dryRun.intro: rob(i) = max(rob it + rob(i+2), skip it = rob(i+1)). Indices past the end return 0.

java.explanation: Base case: walking past the last house yields no money — return 0.
Rob house i, then the next legal house is i+2 — the +2 jump enforces 'no adjacent'.
Best of the two choices. It's max because we maximize loot, not count paths.

python.explanation: Taking house i forces a 2-house jump, baking in the adjacency constraint.
Pick the more profitable branch — max, never sum.

edgeCases.behavior: rob(0) = max(5 + rob(2), rob(1)) = max(5, 0) = 5 — single house is always robbed.

pitfalls: Pulling the rob branch from i+1 instead of i+2 — lets you rob adjacent houses.
Returning a non-zero value past the end — corrupts the base case.
Reaching for a fixed 'alternate houses' greedy — provably wrong on [2,1,1,2].

approaches.name: Top-Down Memoization
approaches.whenToMention: The first fix once you spot the overlap — 'I'll cache rob(i) so each suffix is solved once'.
hints: rob(i) always returns the same number for a given i. How do you avoid recomputing it?
Add a memo array indexed by i. On entry, return the cached value if it exists; otherwise compute and store it.
memo[i] = max(nums[i] + solve(i+2), solve(i+1)), saved before returning.
approaches.complexityReasoning: There are n distinct subproblems (one per starting index). Each is computed once with O(1) work after its children are cached → O(n) time, O(n) for the memo plus recursion stack.
approaches.explanation:
Keep the identical take/skip recurrence, but cache `rob(i)` the first time it's computed. A `memo` array indexed by house starts 'empty'; each call checks the cache before recursing and writes the result before returning.

**The mental shift: the suffix starting at i has one answer, so compute it once.** In the brute force, `rob(2)` might be reached through 'skip 0, skip 1' and again through other branches — each path recomputing the same suffix. Memoizing turns the exponential tree into n unique subproblems, each evaluated a single time.

**Why top-down is the gentle first step.** You don't have to reason about iteration order — the recursion naturally resolves dependencies from the base case outward. You literally take the working recursion, add a cache check at the top and a cache write at the bottom, and the complexity collapses to linear.

**Why the sentinel matters.** Money can be 0, so 0 is a *valid* answer and can't double as 'uncomputed'. Use -1 (loot is never negative) so the cache check never mistakes a real zero answer for a miss.
approaches.insight: Memoization is the bridge every DP problem crosses: it proves your recurrence correct while making it fast, before you ever worry about tabulation or space. If you can write the recursion, you can almost always memoize it mechanically.

dryRun.intro: memo[i] caches the best loot achievable starting at house i. Filled from the back.

java.explanation: -1 marks 'uncomputed'. Critical because 0 is a legitimate loot value and can't double as the sentinel.
Cache hit — return instantly. This guard converts the exponential tree into n one-time computations.
Store the best result for suffix i before returning so it's never recomputed.

python.explanation: Return the cached suffix answer before doing any work.
Memoize the take-or-skip decision for this starting index.

edgeCases.behavior: Every branch is 0, so memo fills with zeros and returns 0 — the -1 sentinel keeps those real zeros distinct from misses.
Caching still lands on 4 (rob ends), proving memoization preserves the optimal, not the greedy, answer.

pitfalls: Using 0 as the uncomputed sentinel — collides with legitimate 0 loot and causes recomputation or wrong reads.
Forgetting to store memo[i] before returning — stays exponential.
Indexing the memo by something other than i — the only state that defines a subproblem here is the starting index.

approaches.name: Bottom-Up — Two Rolling Variables (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: The answer they want. Frame it as 'each house only needs the best totals from one and two houses back, so two variables replace the whole array'.
hints: Build the best-so-far loot from the left. To decide house i, what two running totals do you actually need?
Track rob1 = best up to two houses back, rob2 = best up to the previous house. Robbing the current house adds it to rob1.
Loop the houses: newRob = max(rob2, rob1 + x); then slide rob1 = rob2, rob2 = newRob. Answer is rob2.
approaches.complexityReasoning: One pass over n houses with O(1) work each → O(n) time. Only two integers are kept regardless of n → O(1) space.
approaches.explanation:
Walk the street left to right keeping two running totals: `rob1` is the best loot achievable up to *two* houses ago, and `rob2` is the best up to the *previous* house. At each house with value `x`, the best you can do is either skip it (keep `rob2`) or rob it (`rob1 + x`, since robbing forbids the immediately previous house). Take the max, then slide both variables forward.

**The mental shift: the only history that matters is two totals.** A full `dp[]` array works, but `dp[i]` reads only `dp[i-1]` and `dp[i-2]` — everything older is dead. So `rob1` and `rob2` *are* the DP table, compressed. `rob1 + x` is the 'rob this house' branch because `rob1` deliberately excludes the previous house; `rob2` is the 'skip this house' branch.

**Why this also subsumes the base cases.** Seeding both variables to 0 means an empty street returns 0, and a single house returns `max(0, 0 + nums[0]) = nums[0]` — no special-casing required. The zeros represent 'no money before the street started'.

**Why the slide order matters.** Compute `newRob` from the *current* `rob1` and `rob2` first, then advance `rob1 = rob2` and `rob2 = newRob`. Update them in the wrong order and you'd feed a just-updated value back into the same iteration, double-counting a house. This is the same line-ordering discipline as rolling Fibonacci.
approaches.insight: Once a 1D DP only reaches back a constant number of cells, the array is overkill — keep exactly that many rolling variables. House Robber reaches back two, so two variables give O(1) space. The very same compression powers Climbing Stairs and is the trick interviewers love to see you reach for unprompted.

dryRun.intro: rob1 = best two houses back, rob2 = best previous house. newRob = max(skip, rob this).

java.explanation: rob1 = best up to i-2, rob2 = best up to i-1. Zeros mean 'no money before the street' and handle empty/single-house inputs.
Skip this house (rob2) vs rob it (rob1 + x). rob1 excludes the previous house, so adding x stays legal.
Slide: previous best becomes the new two-back. Must run before rob2 is overwritten.
Advance the running best to include the current house's decision.

python.explanation: Both seeded to 0 — covers empty and single-element inputs without a special case.

python.line: rob1, rob2 = rob2, max(rob2, rob1 + x)
python.explanation: Tuple assignment computes the whole right side from the OLD values first, so the slide is atomic and order-safe.

diagrams.title: Best loot rolling left to right
diagrams.caption: Each cell is the best total considering houses up to that index. Only the trailing two are live.

edgeCases.behavior: Loop never runs, rob2 stays 0 → returns 0. The zero-seed handles empty input for free.

pitfalls: Updating rob2 before rob1 in Java — feeds the new value back in and double-counts the current house.
Returning rob1 instead of rob2 — off-by-one that gives the answer excluding the last house.
Special-casing length 0 and 1 unnecessarily — the zero seeds already cover both.

commonMistakes: Assuming a fixed 'rob every other house' greedy — fails on [2,1,1,2] (returns 3, optimal is 4).
Taking the rob branch from dp[i-1] instead of dp[i-2] — lets you rob adjacent houses.
Using sum instead of max — this maximizes loot, it doesn't count arrangements.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Greedy alternate-house selection
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Robbing strictly every other house ignores that a better combination may skip two in a row. On [2,1,1,2] it picks 2+1=3 but the optimum is 2+2=4.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad: return sum(nums[i] for i in range(0, len(nums), 2))
commonMistakesDetailed.good:
rob1, rob2 = 0, 0
for x in nums:
    rob1, rob2 = rob2, max(rob2, rob1 + x)
return rob2

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Robbing from the wrong predecessor
commonMistakesDetailed.why: When you rob house i you must add the best total that EXCLUDES house i-1 (that's dp[i-2]/rob1). Pulling from dp[i-1] permits robbing adjacent houses.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Slide-order clobber
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Overwriting rob2 before copying it into rob1 destroys the value the next step needs, double-counting the current house.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
rob2 = Math.max(rob2, rob1 + x);
rob1 = rob2;

followupVariations.title: House Robber II
followupVariations.hint: Houses in a circle — first and last are adjacent. Run the linear solver twice: once excluding house 0, once excluding the last, take the max.

followupVariations.title: House Robber III
followupVariations.hint: Houses form a binary tree. Post-order DP returning (rob, skip) pairs per node.

followupVariations.title: Delete and Earn
followupVariations.hint: Bucket values by their total, then it's literally House Robber on the value axis (taking v forbids v-1 and v+1).

followupVariations.title: Climbing Stairs
followupVariations.hint: Same dp[i-1]/dp[i-2] two-back structure and O(1) rolling compression — but it sums to count, while this maxes to optimize.

patternNote: Canonical 1D Dynamic Programming — take-or-skip with an adjacency gap (max-weight independent set on a path). Recognize it whenever choosing an item forbids its neighbor. Same core as House Robber II/III and Delete and Earn.
